title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes and no, thank, apologise and say goodbye in Gujarati.
intro:
Gujaratis greet each other in several ways: the all-purpose **નમસ્તે** *namaste*, the very common devotional **જય શ્રી કૃષ્ણ** *jay shrī kruṣṇa*, and above all the question **કેમ છો?** *kem chho?* 'how are you?', which works almost like 'hello'.

In this unit you also meet the three words for 'you' — the most important politeness choice in Gujarati.

vocab.note: extremely common greeting among Hindu Gujaratis, especially to elders

vocab.en: how are you? (polite) — also used as 'hello'

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb
grammar.body:
Gujarati puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence. The usual order is subject – (time/place) – object – verb. Words that English puts after the verb come before it: 'I drink tea' is હું ચા પીઉં છું *huṃ chā pīuṃ chhuṃ*, literally 'I tea drink am'.

The little word **છે / છું / છો** ('is / am / are') usually comes last. Negation goes before the verb or replaces છે with **નથી** *nathī*.

Questions keep the same order; you just raise your voice at the end or add a question word before the verb.

grammar.title: Three ways to say 'you': તું, તમે, આપ
grammar.body:
Gujarati chooses the word for 'you' by closeness and respect, and the verb changes with it.

**તું** *tuṃ* — intimate: close friends of your age, younger siblings, children, God. Verb: છે, imperative bare stem (બેસ 'sit').
**તમે** *tame* — the normal polite form for any adult, and also the plural 'you all'. Verb: છો, imperative -o (બેસો).
**આપ** *āp* — very respectful: elders you don't know well, officials, customers in formal settings, speeches. It takes the same verb forms as તમે.

When in doubt, use **તમે**. Using તું with a stranger is rude; using આપ with a friend sounds stiff or teasing. Many Gujarati children use તમે even for their parents.

examples.en: Sit. (to a child or close friend)

dialogue.title: Neighbours on the stairs
dialogue.setting: Rameshbhai meets his neighbour Hansaben on the stairs of their Ahmedabad apartment block.

lines.speaker: Hansa
lines.native: જય શ્રી કૃષ્ણ, રમેશભાઈ. કેમ છો?
lines.roman: jay shrī kruṣṇa, Rameshbhāī. kem chho?

lines.speaker: Hansa
lines.native: હું પણ મજામાં. ઘરમાં બધા કેમ છે?
lines.roman: huṃ paṇ majāmāṃ. gharmāṃ badhā kem chhe?
lines.en: I'm fine too. How is everyone at home?

lines.speaker: Hansa
lines.native: સારું. માફ કરજો, મને મોડું થાય છે.
lines.roman: sāruṃ. māf karjo, mane moḍuṃ thāy chhe.

culture: Gujaratis add **-ભાઈ** *-bhāī* ('brother') or **-બેન** *-ben* ('sister') to first names as a friendly, respectful way of addressing adults: Rameshbhai, Hansaben. Elders may be called **કાકા** *kākā* 'uncle' or **માસી** *māsī* 'auntie' even by strangers. **આવજો** 'goodbye' literally means 'please come (again)' — Gujaratis avoid saying 'go' when parting. Muslim Gujaratis typically greet with *salām* / *ādāb*, and Jains often say *jay jinendra*.
